Platform Information Design and Competitive Price Targeting

Ruiqi Wu, Yufeng Huang and Nan Li ∗

May 23, 2025

Abstract

We study platform information design, in which a platform provides information about individual consumers, enabling sellers to set targeted prices. Because targetable information partitions the market and might intensify seller competition, what information should be provided remains an empirical question. We collect novel micro data from Steam, the dominant PC video game platform, and use granular consumer purchase and usage data to estimate their heterogeneous demand for video games. We then develop an equilibrium targeted pricing model to simulate counterfactual outcomes under all possible information designs. We demonstrate that the profit-maximizing information design—which distinguishes heterogeneous consumer types while accounting for the design’s equilibrium impact—yields substantially higher profits compared to demand-based heuristics that ignore the equilibrium impact.

Keywords: information design, competition, price targeting

1 Introduction

A platform collects detailed data on individual consumer behavior across all its third-party sellers.

These comprehensive data allow the platform to pin down each consumer’s preference and price

sensitivity, putting it at a uniquely powerful position: The platform can decide what information

about each consumer to communicate to sellers and what to withhold from sellers, thereby influ-

encing whether and how prices and promotions are targeted to individual or groups of consumers.

In practice, a platform often designs of its infrastructure or rules to influence what information is

used in targeting (Bhargava et al., 2020). For example, advertising platforms such as Google and

Meta provide predefined interest labels about individual consumers, effectively dividing them into

segments. Online retail platforms such as Amazon and eBay are also developing lists of consumer

segments that sellers can target with price promotions or coupons.

Despite the increasing popularity of targeting, platforms do not have a clear understanding on

how they should optimally design targetable segments. From Shopify’s segmentation guidelines to

Google’s Topic API and Facebook’s behavioral taxonomy, practitioners often segment consumers

based on demographics and behavioral metrics, with the intent to group consumers with similar

preferences into the same segment. Whereas these segment designs reflect the established academic

insight that a monopolist can benefit from targeting consumer preferences (Rossi et al., 1996;

Smith et al., 2023; Dub´e and Misra, 2023), they rarely consider the implications on competing

sellers’ equilibrium strategies.

The equilibrium implications of price targeting are important because a segmentation scheme

partitions consumers into submarkets—each with its own local market structure—and consequently

affects competing sellers’ prices and equilibrium outcomes. These equilibrium implications, how-

ever, are nuanced. Theoretical and limited empirical works have shown that the impact of compet-

itive price targeting on profits and welfare are directionally ambiguous (Holmes, 1989; Corts, 1998;

Besanko et al., 2003; Dub´e et al., 2017). In addition, theoretical predictions depend on conditions

that are difficult to verify empirically, and do not easily generalize to realistic platform markets.

Moreover, beyond the binary case of whether or not firms can target, the extant literature is mostly

silent about how targetable segments should be designed.

In this paper, we characterize the platform’s design of targetable segments as an information

design problem, in which the platform-designed segments reveal information about individual con-

1

Page 3

sumer demand to sellers, who then use this information to set optimal targeted prices.1 Using

detailed micro data from Steam, the dominant PC video game platform, our counterfactual simula-

tions demonstrate that incorporating equilibrium considerations is crucial for the optimal platform

information design.

We assemble a novel dataset containing individual-level panel data on consumer purchase and

usage behavior, and game characteristics derived from texts that describe the game’s content and

style. Using these data, we estimate a structural demand model that captures consumers’ joint deci-

sions of purchase and usage, measuring heterogeneous consumer preferences over multi-dimensional

product characteristics. In particular, the model allows consumers’ expected usage to affect their

purchase decisions, thereby uncovering consumer preferences using data on which games they pur-

chase and on how intensively they engage with these games. Our demand estimates identify eight

latent consumer types, who differ in their overall engagement with gaming, tastes for specific game

features, and sensitivities to prices. Importantly, assuming zero marginal costs, our estimates im-

ply equilibrium uniform prices that closely match the observed uniform prices on Steam, lending

credibility to these estimates as the basis of counterfactual equilibrium outcomes.

Next, we develop an equilibrium targeted pricing model to simulate alternative platform in-

formation design scenarios. We extend the standard uniform pricing equilibrium (Berry et al.,

1995)—where sellers are informed about the consumer type distribution but have no information

about individual consumer types—to a targeted pricing equilibrium where sellers also have some

information that allow them to infer each consumer’s type. When all sellers have the same informa-

tion about each consumer, the equilibrium is one where the platform effectively groups consumers

into segments, with sellers competing for each segment as a distinct submarket.2 The model also

generalizes to the case where sellers hold different information about each consumer and thereby

compete in partially overlapping submarkets (see Appendix C).

Our results demonstrate that targeted pricing significantly improves total profits when im-

plemented with the optimal information design—one that maximizes the total profits among the

platform and all sellers. We arrive at this first conclusion by simulating all 4, 140 information

designs, each representing a distinct information set. We find that targeting based on full infor-

mation generates a 2.88% increase in total profits relative to uniform pricing, which is equivalent

2In this case, one can interpret the platform’s information design either as provision of information (which is our primary interpretation) or as a rule that restricts what information price targeting can be based on.

to approximately $124 million per year. However, targeting based on coarse consumer information

generates drastically different market outcomes depending on how the information set is designed.

For example, among all “Coarse 2” designs—allowing just two price segments—the platform can

achieve profit increases over uniform pricing that range from 1.74% to a mere 0.05%, suggesting

that optimal information design plays a critical role given the granularity of targetable information.

We proceed to demonstrate that equilibrium considerations are paramount in obtaining the op-

timal information design. We arrive at this second conclusion by simulating counterfactual designs

of targetable segments based on the grouping of consumer types with similar price elasticity pat-

terns, among other demand-based heuristics. We find that, holding fixed the level of granularity,

these heuristics consistently lead to much less effective targeting than the optimal information de-

sign. For example, with two targetable segments, elasticity-based heuristics yield an approximately

one percentage point lower profits compared to the optimal design, leaving $43 million in annual

profits on the table. This profit gap persists across alternative heuristics and remains robust to

different sources of consumer heterogeneity, demonstrating that demand-based heuristics, which

represent similarity in consumers’ price sensitivities or tastes, fail to approximate the platform’s

optimal design that also accounts for its impact on sellers’ equilibrium strategies.

Beyond the maximization of total profits across the platform and all sellers, we also demonstrate

that the optimal information design substantially improves consumer welfare, the platform’s profit,

and the balance of competition across large versus small sellers, suggesting that well-designed infor-

mation structures can simultaneously benefit a broad set of market participants in the ecosystem.

Our findings offer important managerial implications for platforms that provide consumer in-

formation to sellers. The prior literature emphasizes how a single seller can use advanced models

and rich datasets to uncover individual-level demand heterogeneity, enabling precise targeting of

distinct consumer types. In contrast, we demonstrate that in a marketplace with competing sellers,

the platform must also account for how its information design affects seller competition in equi-

librium. This equilibrium consideration is especially crucial when the platform intends to provide

only a limited number of consumer segments—a likely scenario given practical constraints such

as implementation or menu costs (Sheshinski and Weiss, 1977), privacy concerns (Goldfarb and

Tucker, 2019), and fairness considerations (Kahneman et al., 1986), all of which tend to favor the

provision of few coarsened consumer segments. To this end, we develop an empirical framework

that captures how the information available to competing sellers shapes equilibrium prices, profits,

and consumer surplus. Our framework is generalizable across platforms with diverse consumer

compositions and objectives.

Related Literature. We extend the literature on competitive third-degree price discrimination

by addressing the information design problem faced by online platforms. Prior theoretical work has

shown that targeted pricing can either enhance or harm competing sellers’ profits, depending on the

structure of consumer preference heterogeneity (Thisse and Vives, 1988; Holmes, 1989; Shaffer and

Zhang, 1995; Corts, 1998; Chen and Iyer, 2002; Armstrong, 2006). However, the direction of profit

(and welfare) impacts relies on conditions that are not easy to verify empirically.3 In addition,

existing theoretical findings are typically derived under restrictive assumptions—most notably,

markets with only two single-product sellers and limited forms of consumer heterogeneity—and

do not easily generalize to modern marketplaces characterized by richer consumer heterogeneity

and market structures. In the meantime, a small but growing empirical literature similarly focuses

on settings with two competing firms and limited consumer heterogeneity (Besanko et al., 2003;

Dub´e et al., 2017). Our contribution is twofold. First, we extend the empirical literature to

a more realistic platform setting involving numerous single- and multi-product sellers and multi-

dimensional consumer heterogeneity. Second, we introduce a framework that enables simulations of

counterfactual equilibrium outcomes beyond the boundary cases of full-information and no targeting

to systematically evaluate the continuum of intermediate information designs—where platforms

enable targeting based on partial information about consumers.4

Our paper also contributes to the growing literature on platform information design, particularly

through the design of infrastructure and rules (Bhargava et al., 2020). Most existing studies on

information design focus on providing information to consumers—about sellers or products—often

through mechanisms such as reputation systems, warranties, or quality guarantees (Hui et al.,

2021; Vatter, 2022; Hopenhayn and Saeedi, 2022; Hopenhayn et al., 2022; Hui et al., 2023). In

contrast, we examine the platform’s role in providing information to sellers, specifically shaping

sellers’ beliefs about individual consumers through the design of coarse segmentation. Our focus on

competitive price targeting distinguishes this work from the literature on monetizing data through

targeted advertising (Bergemann and Bonatti, 2024), and our conceptualization of information

design differs from studies on the market for data transactions between sellers and intermediaries

3For example, Corts (1998)’s key condition is whether two competing firms’ rank orders between a “strong” consumer type and a “weak” consumer type coincide, a condition defined on firms’ best response functions between targeted-pricing and uniform-pricing equilibrium.

4While not being their main point, Dub´e et al. (2017) also empirically examine how targeting based on behavioral types or geographic locations affects equilibrium outcomes, answering a question related to ours—which consumer information should sellers target.

(Pancras and Sudhir, 2007; Bergemann and Bonatti, 2015).

Broadly, our empirical study also presents new insights on the pricing of digital content, espe-

cially digital video games (Rao, 2015; Sunada, 2018; Brecko, 2023).

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 conceptualizes the platform information

design problem. Section 3 introduces the context and data. Section 4 sets up the demand and

equilibrium pricing model. Section 5 presents estimation results. Section 6 discusses the value of

information design through counterfactual simulations. Section 7 concludes the paper.

2 Conceptual model: Information and competitive price-targeting

Setup. We present a simple conceptual model to illustrate the importance of accounting for seller

competition in a platform’s information design. Assume that two single-product sellers, A and B,

compete for each consumer, i. The consumer’s utility for product j ∈{A, B} depends on her taste

for the product, βij, a price coefficient normalized to −1, and a type-1 extreme value utility shock:

Uij = βij −Priceij + ϵij. (1)

Consumer taste for each product, βij, is heterogeneous. Assume βij can take either a high value

by preferences (βiA, βiB) = (L, L), (L, H), (H, L), and (H, H), respectively. We set H = 2 and

equation / math rendering (image)
NOTE: contains mathematical notation; text above is the PDF text layer and symbols may be mis-extracted. Image shows the original.

L = 1, and assume each type constitutes 25% of the market. We also assume that sellers know

the value of H and L and the proportion of each consumer type in the market, but not individual

consumer i’s type. Therefore, without additional information, sellers set uniform equilibrium prices

for all consumers based on the distribution of consumer types.

Information design. We assume the platform knows each individual consumer’s type. Because

the platform controls the information environment, it can decide what individual consumer infor-

mation to communicate to sellers, thus allowing them to target groups of consumers using the

information. Formally, we characterize a specific information design as a partition of the set of

consumer types, {1, 2, 3, 4}, where each partition corresponds to a grouping of types into coarsened

segments.

5

Page 7

Given the platform’s information design, sellers update their beliefs about each consumer’s type

based on the segment to which the consumer belongs, and set equilibrium prices accordingly. At one

extreme, the platform can disclose full information about consumer types, designing an information

set {{1}, {2}, {3}, {4}}. In this case, sellers know and can set equilibrium targeted prices for each

consumer type. At the other extreme, the platform can disclose no information about individual

types, designing an information set {{1, 2, 3, 4}}. In this case, sellers must rely solely on their prior

beliefs about the consumer type distribution and set uniform equilibrium prices.

Alternatively, the platform can provide a coarsened information set which reveals certain as-

pect(s) of consumer heterogeneity and conceals other aspects. For example, the platform can

provide information on consumers’ taste for product B while withholding information about con-

sumer taste for product A, designing the information set {{1, 3}, {2, 4}}. In practice, this means

grouping types (L, L) and (H, L) into coarse segment I, and types (L, H) and (H, H) into coarse

segment II, and informing sellers of each segment’s composition. Rational sellers will then infer

that consumers in segment I are equally likely to be type 1 or type 3, with a similar inference for

segment II. Sellers set equilibrium prices for each segment accordingly, following the first-order

conditions detailed in Section 4.2.

information about individual types (information set {{1, 2, 3, 4}}), resulting in sellers setting uni-

form prices. The equilibrium price is $1.59 for all consumers, which falls between the dollar-valued

intercepts $2 and $1 for the two types. The second column presents the opposite scenario where

the platform provides full information, {{1}, {2}, {3}, {4}}. In this case, sellers set prices that

target each consumer type. The way targeted prices differ from uniform prices reflects consumer

heterogeneity. Specifically, both sellers lower the price to $1.40 for type 1 consumers, who have low

preferences for both products, and raise it to $1.60 for type 4 consumers, who have high preferences

for both products. In addition, seller A reduces the price for type 2 consumers, who prefer the

competitor’s product, and raises the price for type 3, who prefer the focal product. Seller B’s prices

are symmetric to A’s.

One might expect targeting to increase profits. However, in this case, full-information targeted

prices in fact reduces profits compared to uniform prices. As shown in Table 2.1, a decomposition

of equilibrium profits by consumer type reveals an interesting pattern: with full information, seller

A’s profits from consumer types 1 and 3—those with lower preferences for seller B—decline by

about 4%. The profit loss arises because seller B, who targets these consumer types with lower

prices ($1.40 for type 1 and $1.32 for type 3), effectively lowers seller A’s residual demand. By

symmetry, the same happens to seller B for types 1 and 2. In other words, although each seller sets

type-specific prices to maximize its own profit from each consumer type, the competitor’s targeting

can lower residual demand, intensify competition, and lead to lower total equilibrium profits. This

finding under competing sellers sharply contrasts with the case with a monopoly seller, where price

targeting never hurts profits (Smith et al., 2023; Dub´e and Misra, 2023).

Profit-maximizing coarsened information design. We further examine the 13 intermediate

cases where the platform limits the consumer information shared with sellers and thus allows only

partial targeting. We refer to these cases as coarsened information designs and present their profit

increase relative to the no-information scenario in Figure 2.1. The design that maximizes total

seller profit is {{1}, {2, 3, 4}}, which increases profits by 0.5% relative to the uniform equilibrium

(1.5% relative to the full-information case). This optimal design separates consumers based on

whether they exhibit a low probability of purchasing either product but pools all other consumers.

As shown in Table 2.1, under full information, seller A significantly loses profit in its stronghold,

type 3, when seller B can poach them with a lower price. By contrast, under optimal coarsened

design, seller B sets a less aggressive price, catering to the coarsened segment {2, 3, 4}, leading

to higher residual demand and profits for the seller A. Along the same line, two other coarsened

designs that pool consumers with distinct tastes also result in profit gains. Conversely, designs that

separate these two consumer types into distinct segments significantly reduce sellers’ profits, with

the least profitable design reducing total profit by 1.5%.

Discussions. Our conceptual and structural model interprets the provision of segment labels as a

source of information, which allows sellers—otherwise with no information about each consumer—

to infer the consumer’s type and set targeted prices. Alternatively, when the same information

is imposed on all sellers, one can interpret the segment labels as a restriction on the aspects of

consumer information that sellers are allowed to target. As a result, sellers set equilibrium prices for

each segmented market, similar to zone pricing in physical retail (Adams and Williams, 2019). This

alternative interpretation is isomorphic in our structural analysis and leads to the same findings.

Moreover, although we abstract away from the specifics of implementation, our proposed in-

formation design framework aligns well with current platform practices and can be supported by

existing technologies. For instance, platforms like Google may assign consumer labels to indicate

individual preferences, while platforms such as Amazon and eBay allow sellers to target pre-defined

consumer groups through their seller interfaces (see Appendix Figure A.1). What may differ from

existing practices is how to define targetable segments. Here, and in our empirical analysis, we

demonstrate that optimal information design should account for its equilibrium impacts.

3 Context, Data, and Descriptive Statistics

3.1 Context: Steam

Steam, owned by Valve Software, is the world’s largest digital marketplace for PC video games. It is

estimated to hold 75% of the market share, offering over 30,000 games, software titles, and add-ons

(Zuckerman, 2020). Consistent with this estimate, Google Trends data show that Steam consis-

tently dominates consumer search interests, indicating limited competition from other platforms

(see Appendix B).

Like other online marketplaces, Steam allows third-party sellers to list games and set their own

prices. These sellers range from major publishers like Ubisoft and Sega to small indie studios with

only a few titles. Consumers can access the platform for free but must purchase games to play them.

Once purchased, a game is added to the user’s library and remains accessible indefinitely. Steam

processes all payment and charges a 30% commission fee from it. Since 2017, this commission has

been Steam’s primary revenue source, with third-party titles accounting for 98% of total transaction

value and Valve’s own games comprising just 2% during our sample period.

We highlight three industry details of Steam that help us study the information design question.

First, because Steam processes all transactions and hosts all gaming sessions, it tracks the entire

game purchases and usage history for each consumer. These micro data contain crucial information

for us to estimate and understand consumer heterogeneity, a critical prerequisite for analyzing the

profitability of price targeting.

Second, Steam does not allow targeted prices or targeted coupons during the sample period.5

The absence of targeting allows us to observe the prices facing all consumers, thereby alleviating

concerns about unobserved discounts that may arise due to targeting.

Third, several institutional features suggest that sellers primarily make pricing decisions to

maximize game sales revenue. In particular, Steam does not sell advertising slots, so sellers do not

make advertising decisions on Steam.6 Additionally, although Steam recommends games based on

individual consumers’ interests, it has explicitly committed to not using prices in the recommen-

5This price uniformity is upheld with rare exceptions. Only one single anecdote exists where a large seller requested Steam to distribute targeted coupons to specific previous buyers, which is outside our sample period. Moreover, there is little anecdotal evidence of sellers circumventing the system by emailing consumers targeted coupons, primarily because Valve does not share consumers’ email address with the publishers. See https://store.steampowered.com/privacy agreement/ for more details.

6Steam’s detailed policy regarding sellers’ advertising and other marketing activities is publicly stated at https:// partner.steamgames.com/doc/marketing/tools.

dation system.7 This fact allows us to abstract away from modeling the effect of prices on Steam’s

recommendation and thus consumers’ consideration sets. Moreover, upfront sales revenue remains

the dominant source of income for sellers: only 3% of games offer in-game purchases, and in-game

advertising is discouraged and has since been banned.8 Further, because Steam distributes digital

game copies via its own servers, sellers face negligible marginal costs (similar to other digital goods,

Rao, 2015). Given these factors, it is plausible to assume that sellers set prices to maximize the

revenue from game sales, thereby allowing for a tractable model to characterize sellers’ equilibrium

pricing behavior.

3.2 Data

Data collection. We collect consumer panel data directly from Steam’s store website, commu-

nity API, and storefront API. We start by randomly sampling one million existing Steam users

in December 2016, with approximately 810,000 (81%) having accessible public accounts.9 Subse-

quently, we narrow down the sample to 131,539 users who owned at least one game and logged in

at least once in December 2016. For this sample, from February 5, 2017, to December 6, 2017, we

track the games in each user’s library and their cumulative playing time on a daily basis. We back

out the purchase history by recording the day a user adds each game to her library, and we compute

daily usage time at the minute level by taking the first difference on the cumulative time.10 We

retain a final sample of 34,548 active users who had positive spending and usage throughout the

sample period and remained on Steam until at least November 2017.

Next, we collect daily price data for the 17,686 games available during the sample period.

We observe both regular prices and the final prices post-discounts. Additionally, we collect the

detailed characteristics of 4,581 popular games, such as developers, publishers, game descriptions,

and user-generated tags, from a third-party data aggregator.11

Measuring product features by meta-tags. A crucial step in our analysis is to characterize

product differentiation. Whereas each game possesses unique content and potentially appeals to a

particular consumer type, it is computationally infeasible to uncover consumer tastes at the product

level, especially with a large number of products.12 To address this challenge, we characterize each

game as a combination of key features that encapsulate its distinct content.

We derive these features from user-generated tags, which reflect each game’s content in detail.

For example, the popular first-person shooter (FPS) game, “Counter Strike: Global Offensive,”

has tags “FPS,” “Shooter,” “Multiplayer,” “Competitive,” “Team-based,” “e-sports,” “Tactical,”

and so on. These tags provide finer-grained information than genres and capture more nuanced

differences across games that are relevant to users’ purchase decisions.13 However, given the 311

unique tags present across all games, estimating heterogeneous consumer preferences in such high

dimensions is challenging. Therefore, we group tags with similar semantic meanings or describe

similar contexts together to reflect the primary elements consumers seek in game content.

We use Global Vectors (GloVe) to capture the meaning of tags (Pennington et al., 2014).

First, we obtain 200-dimensional word embeddings for each tag from a pre-trained GloVe model

based on Twitter data.14 Second, we cluster these word embeddings using a hierarchical clustering

algorithm and manually correct misclassified tags. We then assign a “meta-tag” to each word

cluster, summarizing the common feature described by the words. In total, we define nine meta-

tags and present them in Appendix Table B.1. Each meta-tag is a binary variable indicating

whether any original game tag belongs to the corresponding cluster. Note that these meta-tags

are not mutually exclusive—a game can possess more than one meta-tag if it encompasses multiple

features. On average, a game has 18 original tags and 2.6 meta-tags. In Section 4, we capture

heterogeneous tastes for games using these defined meta-tags.

Market structure. We demonstrate that Steam’s market structure differs significantly from

canonical theory models of targeted pricing, which typically feature two firms that each offer a

single product (Holmes, 1989; Corts, 1998). Figure 3.1 presents the distribution of seller sizes—in

terms of their number of games—and revenue shares. We note that Steam is occupied by a few large,

multi-product sellers and a long tail of small, single-product sellers. The 31 largest sellers, each

with more than 20 games, collectively take 48% of the revenue. In contrast, 1,321 single-product

sellers collectively contribute 21% of the revenue.

Moreover, because the large sellers often house multiple development teams that work concur-

rently on distinct projects, they not only offer a greater number of games but also span a broader

range of product features.15 As shown in Figure 3.2, most of the largest 31 sellers have some games

that cover each of the product attributes, while smaller sellers are more dispersed in the game

features developed. The presence of multi-product sellers and product differentiation within each

seller brings forth a more complicated setting, one where existing theories do not apply. Thus,

15As an example, as of May 2021, Ubisoft employs over 20,000 individuals across more than 45 studios.

Consumer heterogeneity. We explore the behavior of active Steam users using the individual

panel data and present the summary statistics in Table 3.1. Notably, consumers are highly engaged

with Steam—over the ten-month sample period, a user logs into the platform for 44.8% days (about

three times a week), spends $157, purchases 16 games, plays 17 games, and spends 1.5 hours playing

games per day on average. The users are generally sensitive to price changes, with 41.1% purchases

made at regular prices, 29.9% on discount, and 29.8% for free games on average. Users also display

general preferences for games with certain meta-tags, such as multiplayer, military, and fantasy,

over other meta-tags, such as team, adventure, or anime.

Moreover, the interquartile ranges in Table 3.1 reveal considerable heterogeneity among users

in the three behavioral aspects—overall engagement, price sensitivity, and tastes in-game features.

The overall engagement differs sharply across users. In the bottom quartile, consumers log in less

than twice a week, spends $32 dollars, plays for 0.6 hour daily, purchases 4 games, and plays only

Current pricing. Our primary source of price variation comes from the temporal price changes

within each game. On Steam, sellers adjust prices by altering regular prices or setting temporary

We highlight two noteworthy observations. First, regular prices for most games rarely change.

During our sample period, on average, a game is on discount 11% of the time, with an average

platform-wide sales event, and the rest of the discounts occur outside the sales event window

throughout the year. Appendix Figure B.5 presents the pricing pattern of a game as a visual

representation.

We leverage sharp price discounts to identify price sensitivities.18 By combining the price panel

with the consumer panel of purchases, we identify consumers’ heterogeneous price sensitivities from

how individual demand co-move with prices within short time windows. We present further details

on pricing patterns and discussions about the identification in Appendix B.4.

4 Structural Model

4.1 Demand: consumer purchase and usage decisions

Overview. We model consumers’ joint purchase and usage behavior using a two-stage framework.

Similar to Crawford and Yurukoglu (2012), our model links purchase decisions to expected usage by

assuming consumers are willing to pay more for games that they anticipate using more frequently.

18We abstract away from price variations across geographic regions (e.g., U.S. or Europe), as we solely observe price series in U.S. stores. Nevertheless, we collect cross-region prices for all games included for structural estimation. The timing and depth of discounts are highly aligned across geographic regions, with a median cross-region weekly price correlation of 0.90, alleviating concern about the impact of cross-region price differences on our estimates. We also abstract away from bundling, as it requires modeling consumer purchases over a bundle of products and increases the computational burden. An examination of available bundles during our estimation period revealed that this practice was not prevalent among games in our estimation sample.

15

Page 17

In the data, purchases are less frequent than usage due to the durable nature of video games. As

such, jointly modeling the two decisions enables us to leverage both decisions to capture consumer

heterogeneity.

We illustrate the timing of a consumer’s two-stage decision in Figure 4.1. The consumer starts

a week with a set of games she already owns, which we refer to as her “library.” She faces two

purchase occasions, each of which allows her to purchase a game from the set of available (but not

yet purchased) games and expand her library. Subsequently, on each day of the week, the consumer

faces two usage occasions, each of which she can decide which game in her library to play and for

how long. Figure 4.1 shows an example: with Games 1 and 2 in her library at the beginning of the

week, the consumer considers buying Games 3, 4, both, or neither. If she purchases Game 3, she

will decide how to allocate time among Games 1, 2, and 3 or other activities every day of the week.

In the above, Uijt is the utility to play game j for hijt hours, a function of the consumer’s persistent

preferences and utility shocks. cthi0t is the consumer’s utility from spending time hi0t on non-

gaming activities, from which she derives utility of ct per hour. The time allocation problem

has three constraints: a time-budget constraint, a non-negativity constraint, and a positive outside

good constraint (one cannot spend all day gaming). The first two constraints are naturally satisfied

given any time allocations. The third constraint holds for more than 99% of all consumer-day level

observations.

Given these constraints, the usage decision in occasion t can be decomposed into two sequential

stages: first, the consumer chooses which game to play; second, she decides how much time to

allocate to the chosen game. We parameterize the utility function based on the multiple discrete-

continuous (MDC) utility specifications in Bhat (2018).

Purchase stage. Consumer i has two purchase occasions at the beginning of each week, and we

denote a week–purchase-occasion combination tw. We assume the consumer explicitly accounts for

the changes in game library, and the associated usage decisions and payoffs, in the week following

a purchase decision. That is, whether to purchase a game depends on how the expected maximum

future payoff in the following week changes with the addition of the game. However, to maintain

model tractability, we do not explicitly characterize the consumer’s expectations of one purchase’s

influence on the other purchase occasions or subsequent usages beyond the week. Instead, we cap-

ture these values (and other potential drivers of purchase beyond the week’s usage) with additional

terms in the utility function. Formally, the consumer chooses among the outside goods and the

available games she has not owned (j ∈{0} ∪Jtw\Litw−1), solving

We then use a latent-class model to capture unobserved heterogeneity across consumers, al-

lowing arbitrary correlation among the heterogeneous parameters (Kamakura and Russell, 1989).

Specifically, we denote r = 1, 2, ..., R as discrete consumer types in the market and and ψr as the

population share of type r. We allow for persistent heterogeneity across consumers in their overall

engagement with gaming, preferences for game features, and price sensitivities. In Table 4.1, Xj

includes a common intercept and the set of meta-tags representing game features, as constructed in

Section 3. The parameter vectors λr(i) and βr(i) capture the preferences of consumer type r(i) for

gaming in general and for specific game features in the usage and purchase stages, respectively. We

also allow price sensitivities, αr(i), to vary by consumer type and interact with game features.20

We identify the usage-stage parameters {η, λ, γ, cwkd, csmr, chld} from consumers’ choices of

what to play and how long to play. Specifically, γ is identified by the typical duration of game-play

across all titles, while ηj and λr are identified through variation in the frequency and duration of

game-play across games with distinct features. In contrast, we identify purchase-stage parameters

δj and βr’s from the deviations between consumers’ purchase decisions and their expected usage

values. For example, a consumer who frequently purchases games she rarely plays likely places

high value on certain game features at the time of purchase. Price sensitivities are identified by

consumers’ responses to sharp discounts, which are the predominant source of price variation in the

data. Temporal variation in consumer behavior helps identify the time shifters—weekend, summer,

20Allowing the price sensitivities to vary by game features fits the data considerably better. A plausible explanation is that, due to the recommendation system, consumers may be more frequently exposed to certain games than others. Games not surfaced to a consumer may not enter her consideration set, thereby reducing her responsiveness to discounts on those games. Because our primary focus is not on why consumers react to certain price discounts more than others, and because prices do not enter the recommendation system (Section 3.1), we take the different price responsiveness as given and capture it in a descriptive way.

and holiday effects for usage, and sales event effects for purchases.

Although we cannot identify the exact number of latent types in the market, we gradually

increase the value of R and compare the corresponding model fit. We set R = 8 because it provides

a good fit to the observed behavior while keeping the computational burden manageable, as later

discussed in Section 5. Given R, we identify latent consumer types leveraging the long panel

structure of our micro data, in which we observe, per consumer, 43 weeks of purchases and 244

days of usage, and up to two purchase or usage occasions per week or day.

Due to computational constraints, we cannot estimate the model on our full dataset. Instead,

we construct a subsample that focuses on popular games during the sample period. Specifically, we

select 171 focal games that constitute a substantial share of revenue or usage time and randomly

sample 6,314 active consumers. The game sample captures the key fraction of the market, with

9 games from Valve, 72 games from 16 large third-party publishers, and 90 games from 88 small

third-party studios. We verify that our feature construction (Section 3) captures the diversified

content of the focal games: on average, each title carries 25 original tags and 4 meta-tags, and

across the 171 games, there are 97 unique meta-tag combinations. See Appendix D.1 for details on

the sampling process.

We aggregate all other games into a “fringe game.” We abstract away from the game features

for the fringe games, normalize their prices to be 0, and introduce (i) a fringe-game fixed effect

and (ii) random coefficients on the fringe game at both the purchase and usage stages. These

21

Page 23

terms allow us to capture heterogeneity in consumers’ tendencies to buy or play fringe games while

preserving model traceability.

Discussions. We now discuss the simplifying assumptions we have imposed to maintain model

tractability. First, we assume the consumer has two purchase occasions per week and two usage

occasions per day. The assumption is consistent with the vast majority of consumers’ choices in the

structural sample: 97% of the consumer-week observations have two or fewer game purchases (95%

conditional on at least one purchase), and 97% of the consumer-day observations involve playing

two or fewer games (92% conditional on positive play time).21

Second, we assume each purchase decision explicitly accounts for its impact on usage only in

the following week. This assumption rules out dynamic purchase decisions, such as stockpiling,

and thus maintains a tractable, static model. This assumption is plausible given the short gap

between a consumer’s purchase time and her initial playing session: of all observations of consumer

purchase and initial game-play, only 11% start more than seven days after purchase. If stockpiling

were prevalent, one would expect a larger share of purchases to exhibit longer delays before initial

usage. In addition, stockpiling would imply intertemporal substitution around major sales events,

as consumers might delay purchases in anticipation of substantial discounts. However, as shown in

Appendix B, estimated price sensitivities remain similar regardless of whether we control for the

timing of platform-wide sales events. Moreover, post-estimation analysis reveals no evidence of a

dip in the purchase shifter prior to sales events.

Third, we assume consumers’ initial game libraries as exogenously given. One may be concerned

that game libraries are selected based on consumers’ unobserved heterogeneity. However, explicitly

modeling these initial libraries is computationally infeasible.22 Nevertheless, we show that most

consumers own a small fraction of the focal set of games, so the initial libraries do not vary

significantly across consumers to cause a meaningful selection bias. On average, consumers own 13

of the 171 focal games (median = 10; IQR = 5–18) before the sample starts. In Appendix C.1,

21We do impose that the two purchase occasions are independent, implicitly assuming that when making the first purchase in a week, the consumer does not account for the possibility that she may buy another game in the same week. This simplifying assumption avoids modeling dynamic purchase decisions and makes the model tractable. We note that only in 3% of the weekly observations does the consumer purchase two games, suggesting that this assumption is not crucial. Moreover, these stats hold across the full sample of active Steam users and titles, confirming that the independence assumption is consistent with typical behavior on Steam.

22It is computationally infeasible for two reasons. First, the set of games is large, leading to a large number of possible libraries (as the combination of owned games) and even larger number of possible paths to reach a given library. Second, because libraries evolve non-stationarily, standard approaches for imposing a stationary initialcondition distribution (e.g., Simonov et al. 2020) do not apply.

22

Page 24

we conduct Monte Carlo simulations and show that demand parameters can be recovered when a

similar fraction of games are purchased before the estimation sample begins. As such, we believe

that assuming exogenous libraries does not lead to a significant bias in our demand estimates.

Fourth, we assume the consumer makes informed purchase decisions, abstracting away from

uncertainty about game quality or match values. We consider this assumption plausible, due to

the abundant information available at the time of purchase, including extensive user reviews on

Steam, gameplay videos on YouTube (Li et al., 2025), and live streams from game influencers

(Huang and Morozov, 2025). Furthermore, despite Steam’s generous return policy, only 3.8% of

the initial purchases are returned in our sample. The lack of return suggests that consumers have

limited uncertainty about game quality at the time of purchase, and thus have no regret after

they begin playing the game.23 Nevertheless, we do allow for discrepancies between purchase- and

usage-stage payoffs, and as we discuss later, these additional terms could capture some extent of

information differences. We also argue that consumers are unlikely to learn about their own match

value to game features over time, because consumers in our sample are experienced gamers. In our

sample, the average consumer has been a player on Steam for 4.3 years (median 3.6 years) prior to

the sample period, and therefore likely know their own preferences over different kinds of games.

Consistent with this conjecture, the distributions of the features among consumers’ first five and

last five purchases are remarkably similar (see Appendix Figure B.3).

Finally, a variety of other factors may also influence consumer demand, including utility directly

from ownership, advertising outside of Steam, personalized recommendations from Steam, learning

of game content post-purchase, and future usage utility beyond the one-week horizon. Abaluck et al.

(2022) argue that if the goal is to characterize equilibrium outcomes under counterfactual scenarios

when demand is held fixed, one can model demand flexibly rather than separating preferences

from alternative demand-driving mechanisms. In our case, we lack data to directly measure these

channels. So, instead of modeling these channels explicitly, we capture them by parameters δj, λr,

and αr—the coefficients that capture differences in purchase behavior (at the game and feature

level) that are not absorbed by expected usage. Accordingly, the results in Section 6 should be

interpreted as the effect of information design conditional on the existing levels of ownership utility,

external advertising, Steam’s recommendation algorithm, post-purchase learning, and any usage

utility beyond one week.

23We infer returns by observations where a game, which was in a user’s library at a certain date, disappears from the library later. In our estimation, we exclude the purchase and usage of the returned games.

4.2 Supply: information, targeting, and equilibrium pricing

This section presents the supply model used to simulate equilibrium targeted prices, which in turn

determine key market outcomes such as profits and consumer surplus under alternative designs.

Information design. Given that the platform observes the complete purchase and usage histories

of each consumer i, we assume—and later verify—that it can accurately determine each individual’s

true type, r(i) ∈{1, ..., R}. The platform then decides what information to disclose to sellers for

targeting individual consumers. Following Section 2, we characterize a platform’s information

design as choosing a partition of the set {1, ..., R}, which we denote as CRx.

Under full information, the platform discloses the exact type of each consumer, so CRfull =

{{1}, . . . , {R}}. Under no information, all consumers are pooled together, and CRnone = {{1, . . . , R}}.

equation / math rendering (image)
NOTE: contains mathematical notation; text above is the PDF text layer and symbols may be mis-extracted. Image shows the original.

Between these two extremes, the platform may choose to disclose partial information by grouping

types into coarsened segments. For example, grouping types 1 and 2 together and the rest sep-

arately corresponds to CRx = {{1, 2}, {3, . . . , R}}. The platform enforces its chosen information

set across all sellers and overrides any information sellers may otherwise possess about individual

consumers. The enforcement can be implemented through labeling consumers or seller interface

design, as described in Appendix A.1.

Using equation (15), we solve the equilibrium price vector under each possible information

design CRx, based on the R consumer types estimated following Section 4.2.25 Following Berry

et al. (1995), we assume the existence of a pure strategy equilibrium and verify this assumption

25In all counterfactual simulations, we solve for the equilibrium prices for each week and then average these prices across weeks. We verify that this approach produces similar results to an alternative where we first aggregate demand across weeks and then solve for one static price vector for the entire sample.

Page 27

numerically. Our numerical results also indicate that the equilibrium is unique: using 100 different

initial price vectors drawn from a Halton sequence, we find that all starting prices converge to the

same solution.26

Discussions. We now discuss several assumptions on the supply side model, imposed to maintain

tractability. First, we assume that all sellers know the true distribution of consumer types—that is,

the primitives and the population share of each type—and use this information to calculate expected

profits. This assumption is standard in the literature (e.g., Berry et al., 1995) and is plausible in our

context, given the maturity of the video game market, the availability of accessible industry reports,

and the experience level of participating sellers. Even small studios typically employ professionals

with years of industry experience (Carter, 2024; Clement, 2024; MarketResearch, 2025).

Second, we focus on platform information designs in which information about individual con-

sumers is kept symmetric across sellers. These symmetric designs closely resemble common industry

practices, where platforms provide a standard seller interface featuring a common list of consumer

segments or a standardized set of consumer labels for targeting. We assume that the use of such

common information set is strictly enforced through platform technology, which also serve as a

commitment device: all sellers share the belief that no one can bypass the restrictions to target

individual consumers. Nevertheless, our equilibrium framework can be naturally extended to set-

tings where sellers have and can use different information to infer consumer types, provided there

is common knowledge of all competing sellers’ information sets. We present this more general case

in Appendix D and presents a specific example of extreme asymmetry in information between large

and small sellers in Section 6.

Third, we assume that sellers maximize profits from upfront sales each week, abstracting away

from in-game purchases, in-game advertising, and dynamic pricing. This assumption enables us

to simulate equilibrium outcomes across an exhaustive range of information designs while accom-

modating a reasonably large number of sellers and products, complex market structures, and rich

consumer heterogeneity across multiple dimensions. Other than being necessary, this assumption

is also plausible in our context. As discussed in Section 3, few games on Steam offer in-game

purchases or carry in-game advertising. Furthermore, as discussed in Section 3 and Appendix B,

the extent of price decline over time-since-launch is very small, suggesting a limited extent of price

skimming (Nair, 2007) in this context.

26We conduct this analysis for all focal equilibria discussed in Section 6, including the full-information case, the no-information case, and the optimally coarsened information designs.

26

Page 28

Finally, one might wonder whether consumers would perceive targeted prices as unfair (Kahne-

man et al., 1986) and consequently churn from the market. Although we do not explicitly model

sellers’ decisions regarding regular pricing versus discounts, we envision that platforms implement

targeted pricing through the distribution of personalized coupons or discounts, which potentially

alleviates consumers’ animosity when they are charged a different regular price than the others.

We interpret the segment-specific prices as effective prices net of discounts, following Besanko et al.

(2003); Dub´e et al. (2017); Shiller (2020); Smith et al. (2023). Specifically, a seller could set the

regular price at the highest targeted price level and issue discounts to the remaining consumer

segments. Additionally, although our model does not explicitly incorporate consumer fairness con-

cerns, we address this issue by showing in Section 6 that the optimal coarsened information designs

we propose help alleviate potential fairness concerns by reducing the dispersion in effective prices.

5 Estimation results

We present the composition of consumer types and their heterogeneity based on our estimated

latent class model with R = 8. We select R = 8 as our final specification because it provides a good

fit to the observed behavior (see Appendix Table C.2) while keeping the computational burden

manageable. Note that the number of information designs, and hence the computation burden in

counterfactual simulations, increases super-exponentially with the number of types. For instance,

increasing the number of types to R = 9 would increase the number of possible information designs

from 4, 140 to 21, 147.27

We report the full set of parameter estimates for Θ1 and Θ2 in Appendix D. In this section, we

discuss the heterogeneity across consumer types, evaluate our model fit, and examine the model-

implied price elasticities.

Consumer heterogeneity. We first summarize the heterogeneity in the overall engagement

across latent consumer types. Figure 5.1 presents, for each consumer type (labeled 1 to 8), the

model-implied average purchase probability across all games in panel (b) and the average price sen-

sitivity in panel (c). We observe substantial heterogeneity reflected in both measures. In particular,

Type 1 consumers (14% of the market) exhibit the highest level of purchase probability, buying

more than one game per month on average. They are also the least price sensitive, with an average

27The number of possible information designs corresponds to the Bell number, which grows super-exponentially with the number of consumer types, as discussed in Appendix A.2.

27

Page 29

price sensitivity of −0.04. Meanwhile, Types 2 and 8 (collectively 30% of the market) purchase

games far less frequently, averaging one every three months, and display moderate price sensitiv-

ities. In contrast, Types 4 and 7 (16% of the market) are the most price-sensitive types—almost

twice as price sensitive as Type 1 consumers—while purchasing games half as often.

Panel (a) shows the fraction of consumers belonging to each type; panel (b) reports the model-implied probability that each type purchases any game; and panel (c) displays the average price sensitivity across all games for each type.

We then explore consumer heterogeneity in tastes for game features. Figure 5.2 presents the

fraction of purchases with the three most popular features—“fantasy,” “multiplayer,” and “mili-

tary.” We find that consumer preferences differ markedly toward game features. Moreover, there is

a correlation between the horizontal and vertical dimensions of consumer heterogeneity—namely,

between feature preferences and overall engagement levels. For example, Type 8 consumers, the

least engaged consumer type, display a clear preference toward games with the “multiplayer” and

“military” feature. Types 1 and 6, both highly engaged, disproportionately favor games with the

“fantasy” feature in purchases. Meanwhile, preferences also diverge across types for other features

such as “team,” “adventure,” “survival,” and “dark,” as suggested by Tables in Appendix D.2.

As discussed in Section 4.1, the model estimates capture not only inherent heterogeneity in

consumer demand but also the influence of demand shifters through other channels. Although our

model remains largely agnostic about the exact mechanism(s) shaping consumer demand, we fur-

ther investigate the relationship between usage-stage and purchase-stage coefficients in Appendix

D. The observed correlation suggests that these parameters likely reflect variation in consumers’

consideration sets. Specifically, consumers are more price sensitive to games with the features

they prefer to purchase and play, indicating that they pay more attention to the prices of games

28

Page 30

with higher match values. This pattern aligns with Steam’s recommendation algorithms, which

tailor game displays based on users’ purchase and usage histories—both reflective of persistent

heterogeneity. In our counterfactual simulations of alternative information designs, we assume con-

sumers’ consideration process is table, which is plausible given that the recommendation algorithm

is independent of market prices.

model-predicted one. As shown in Figure 5.3, our model closely matches the type-specific purchase

patterns overall and across games with different features.

Further, we also show that the optimal uniform equilibrium prices match with the observed

prices on Steam during our sample period. We compute equilibrium prices using our demand

estimates and assuming all sellers set revenue-maximizing uniform prices according to equation

(15). We demonstrate in Table 5.1 that the model-implied equilibrium prices match well with the

similar between model-implied and observed values, and so are the revenue distribution between

large and small sellers and the platform. These results suggest that our demand model and the

equilibrium pricing model provides a good approximation to the observed market outcomes.

It may appear that the elasticity matrix presented in Figure 5.4 is sufficient to inform the

platform’s information design for targeted pricing. After all, absent seller competition, a game’s

own-price elasticities across consumer types could directly inform how that game should vary prices

by consumer. However, our model estimates imply that, on average, removing a game from the

market results in 18% of its market share being diverted to other games. This diversion ratio varies

significantly across consumer types—ranging from 7% to 28%—with Type 1 consumers exhibiting

the highest diversion, suggesting that competition is intense for this highly engaged consumer

type. When information design segments the market into submarkets (e.g., if it isolates Type 1

into its own submarket), it changes the intensity of competition in each submarket and among

different sellers. Therefore, information design potentially has an important impact on competing

sellers’ pricing strategies. In the next section (Section 6), we demonstrate the importance of these

equilibrium considerations.

6 Designing Sellers’ Information for Price Targeting

Combining the demand estimates from Section 5 with the equilibrium pricing model in Section 4.2,

we exhaustively simulate counterfactual equilibrium outcomes across all possible information de-

signs. We begin by evaluating how information design impacts profits at varying levels of granularity

of segmentation (Section 6.1). We focus on the combined profits of itself and all third-party sellers,

because third-party sellers account for 98% of total transaction value (Section 3), and the platform

charges 30% of commission fees over this value, essentially aligning the platform’s profit with sellers’

total profits. Next, we demonstrate that segmenting types using demand-based heuristics alone fails

to approximate the profit increases achieved by the optimal, profit-maximizing, information design

(Section 6.2). We then demonstrate the robustness of our key finding—the necessity of accounting

for seller competition—across alternative distributions of consumer heterogeneity (Section 6.3) and

under objectives different from total profits (Section 6.4).

6.1 The profit impact of platform information design

We begin by evaluating all 4, 140 possible information designs, each as a distinct way of partitioning

the eight consumer types into segments. In practice, a platform may prefer a limited number of

coarse segments to reduce implementation or menu costs (Sheshinski and Weiss, 1977), protect

consumer privacy (Goldfarb and Tucker, 2019),29 or address fairness concerns (Kahneman et al.,

1986) by restricting price dispersion. As such, we focus on comparing information designs with

the same number of segments n (denoted as “Coarse n”)—different information designs with a

similar level of granularity. Figure 6.1 presents the distribution of the percentage increase in total

market profits achieved by various “Coarse n” designs relative to the no-information benchmark

(uniform pricing equilibrium). Note that “Coarse 8” design is equivalent to full information price

targeting, where all sellers can target the true type of each consumer. “Coarse 2” to “Coarse 7”

designs involve the platform grouping some consumers into coarsened segments, allowing sellers to

set targeted prices based on partial consumer information.

We highlight two observations in Figure 6.1. First, price targeting under any information design

yields positive incremental profits relative to uniform pricing. The highest profits arise from full-

information targeting—the most granular design—which increases total seller profits by 2.88%.

29For instance, as described in Appendix A.1, Google’s switching from FLoC to the Topics API reduces the granularity of consumer information by replacing fine-grained behavioral cohorts with broader, rotating interest categories, enhancing privacy while preserving targeting utility.

33

Page 35

The profit increase translates to approximately $123.8 million in additional annual profits based

on Steam’s estimated $4.3 billion total revenue in 2017.30 This substantial profit increase suggests

that targeted prices’ ability to capture consumer heterogeneity outweighs their impact on price

competition, alleviating concerns about intensified competition when sellers target (see Holmes

1989; Corts 1998; Dub´e et al. 2017, and our conceptual example in Section 2).

Second, whereas targeting under any information design improves profits directionally, the

magnitude of profit increase varies substantially across specific designs, even when the granularity,

n is held constant. As illustrated by the box plots in Figure 6.1, the median percentage profit

increase across all possible “Coarse 2” designs is only 0.45%, with the minimum being 0.05%, both

substantially below the 1.74% achieved by the optimal “Coarse 2” design. Likewise, “Coarse 3”

and “Coarse 4” designs’ median profit increases are 0.96% and 1.41%, respectively, with minimum

increases of just 0.17% and 0.39%—much lower than the optimal “Coarse 2” design. These patterns

underscore that platform information design is not merely about the granularity of segmentation.

Rather, how to segment given the granularity can substantially affect the incremental profit from

targeting.

6.2 Understanding the importance of equilibrium considerations

We have shown that, given the number of segments n, the optimal (total-profit-maximizing) design,

identified through counterfactual simulations that explicitly account for each information design’s

impact on equilibrium pricing strategies, generates substantially higher profits than most alternative

designs. This finding leads to a natural question: how important is equilibrium consideration in

information design? Can practitioners use demand heuristics to achieve comparable performance?

To answer this question, we use a heuristic approach that clusters consumer types into coarse

segments solely on the similarity of their own-price elasticities across video games. Specifically, for

each n, we calculate pairwise Euclidean distances between the type-specific elasticity vectors and

then apply k-means clustering to minimize the within-cluster sum of squared distances. Because

own-price elasticity is closely related to optimal single-product pricing, this procedure ensures that

types that are grouped into the same segment are similar in the demand metric that is relevant to

most games’ pricing.31 We present the profit increases achieved by this elasticity-based heuristic

using the steelblue squares in Figure 6.1.

We find that elasticity-based heuristic designs consistently underperform the optimal informa-

tion designs for each level of granularity n. The profit gap is especially pronounced when n is

small—cases in which the platform deliberately limits seller information through coarsened seg-

ments with low granularity. For “Coarse 2” to “Coarse 4” designs, the gap in percentage profit

increase is approximately one percentage point, corresponding to annual profit differences of $42–44

million. As granularity increases, the gap narrows but remains substantial; even with “Coarse 7,”

the profit gap is 0.17 percentage points, or roughly $7.3 million annually.

We then present what segments are formed under the elasticity-based heuristic approach and

our optimal information designs in Table 6.1. The differences between the two approaches are

evident. Elasticity-based heuristics tend to isolate consumer type(s) that exhibit distinct elasticity

patterns from the rest of the consumer types. By contrast, the optimal designs sometimes pool

these distinct types with others. For instance, the heuristic “Coarse 2” design separates Type

7—the most price-elastic group for most games—from the other types. In contrast, the optimal

design combines Type 7 with four other types that are closer in the average price elasticity level

but differ in their preferences for specific game features. This result deviates from the intuition

from monopolistic pricing settings, where recent literature emphasizes isolating distinct consumer

31Visually, this clustering approach is akin to finding similarly colored rows in Figure 5.4

35

Page 37

types using increasingly rich demand-side variables or advanced models to estimate heterogeneous

preferences or treatment effects precisely (Shiller, 2020; Smith et al., 2023; Zhang and Misra, 2022).

With competing sellers, however, optimal information design for price targeting must account for

the nuanced impact of segmentation on how sellers compete “locally” within each segment, and

hence their competitive pricing strategies.

One might question whether own-price elasticities across games are the most appropriate metric

for capturing demand heterogeneity across consumer types. To address this, we further construct

two alternative demand-based heuristics. First, we cluster consumer types based on their type-

specific demand parameters (βr, αr, and γr). Second, we cluster based on rescaled own-price

elasticities, which adjust for the differences in price elasticities across games.32 The left panel of

Figure 6.2 shows that neither of the two alternative measures (“para” and “rescaled elas”) aligns

with the optimal information design and, as we demonstrate later, neither consistently approximates

the optimal design across alternative demand structures. These results further underscore that

segmenting consumers based solely on similarities in preferences or price elasticities is insufficient

for effective information design.

One might further conjecture that heuristics incorporating some supply-side factors—such as

the distribution of competing sellers and the positioning of differentiated products in the product

feature space—could help approximate the optimal design without simulating all counterfactual

information designs. A natural heuristic that reflects these considerations is to cluster consumers

based on their type-specific equilibrium prices under full information. These prices capture both

demand heterogeneity and equilibrium pricing incentives under the most granular information de-

sign. However, as shown in the left panel of Figure 6.2, this approach still underperforms the

optimal information design. We conjecture that this gap persists because coarsened information

designs induce equilibrium price responses that are specific to the coarse market partitions they

create. Hence, they cannot be inferred from the equilibrium prices under full information, which

only captures the competition under a specific information design.

6.3 Unpacking consumer heterogeneity

How do different components of consumer heterogeneity contribute to the profit gap between the

heuristic approach and the optimal information design? Is there a specific dimension of consumer

heterogeneity that drives the previous findings? To answer these questions, we examine counter-

factual equilibrium outcomes under optimal information designs and heuristics-based designs when

consumer heterogeneity is limited to a single dimension.

Guided by two different theoretical frameworks, we decompose consumer heterogeneity into

32Specifically, for each game j, we rescale the own-price elasticities by dividing each type’s elasticity by the elasticity of the most price-sensitive type for that game: ˜ηjjr = −ηjjr/ maxr |ηr

jj|. Visually, this clustering approach is similar to finding similarly colored rows in Figure D.3. The darker tiles indicate higher relative elasticity—i.e., greater price sensitivity compared to other types—for a given game.

37

Page 39

two dimensions: vertical and horizontal heterogeneity. To isolate the vertical dimension, we retain

only the differences in average engagement and price sensitivity across types while removing all

feature-specific taste shifters. This consumer composition mirrors the set-up in Holmes (1989),

where consumers differ only vertically and all sellers compete for the same “strong” versus “weak”

markets. To isolate the horizontal dimension, we equalize average engagement and price sensitivity

across types but preserve variation in taste for specific game features. This consumer composition

mirrors the set-up in Thisse and Vives (1988) and Corts (1998), where sellers have asymmetric

incentives to target consumer types—that is, one game’s “strong” market may be another game’s

“weak” market. In Appendix Figure D.4, we visualize the elasticity patterns corresponding to the

two counterfactual consumer compositions.

Despite that the eight consumer types differ along both vertical and horizontal dimensions,

we find that vertical heterogeneity is the primary driver of profit increases in Steam’s market.

As shown in Figure 6.3, targeting based on full information about vertical heterogeneity yields a

1.73% increase in total market profits relative to uniform pricing. In contrast, targeting based solely

on horizontal preference heterogeneity leads to a more modest 0.96% increase. Nevertheless, the

positive profit impact under purely horizontal heterogeneity alleviates concerns that asymmetric

rankings of “strong” versus “weak” markets across sellers will lead to profit losses under targeted

pricing (Corts, 1998; Dub´e et al., 2017).

we do observe that segmentation using full-information equilibrium prices is closer to the optimal

information design, especially when consumer heterogeneity is purely vertical. Taken together,

these findings underscore the critical importance of incorporating supply-side considerations when

designing information for competing sellers, even when consumer heterogeneity is relatively simple

and limited to a single dimension.

6.4 Other platform objectives

Our earlier analyses in Sections 6.1 through 6.3 have focused on total profits as the primary platform

objective. However, it is important to note that our equilibrium framework can also be used

to evaluate alternative platform objectives that depend on equilibrium prices. In this section,

we examine how well the optimal information design for n = 2—selected by maximizing total

platform and seller profits—aligns with other objectives the platform may value. Specifically, we

consider three alternative objectives that reflect long-term platform goals or potential incentive

misalignments: (1) consumer welfare, (2) profit redistribution between large and small sellers, and

(3) the platform’s own profit, which includes 100% of profits from Valve’s own games and 30% of

profits from third-party titles.

Consumer welfare. The platform may care about consumer welfare, which could affect user

retention and, in turn, platform growth in the long run. We measure consumer welfare as the

inclusive value of owning video games and compare the changes in welfare under targeting relative

to the uniform pricing equilibrium.33 Figure 6.4 presents these changes across three information

33We do acknowledge that our consumer welfare calculation assumes the estimated demand parameters reflect true underlying preferences, an assumption not required for evaluating counterfactual prices and profits under different

39

Page 41

designs: the elasticity-based heuristic “Coarse 2” design, the optimal “Coarse 2” design, and the

full information design. We find that full information design increases consumer welfare by 115

utils, representing a 1.72% improvement over the uniform pricing baseline of 6,685 utils. Notably,

the optimal “Coarse 2” design captures most of the welfare increase despite its reduced granularity.

In contrast, the heuristic “Coarse 2” design yields little to no improvement in consumer welfare

relative to the baseline, despite its same level of granularity as the optimal “Coarse 2” design.

Figure 6.4: Consumer Welfare Change Relative to the Uniform Pricing Benchmark (in Utils)

What makes the profit-maximizing optimal “Coarse 2” design also effective in improving con-

sumer welfare? In Appendix Table D.7, we further examine how each information design impacts

each consumer type. We find that the optimal “Coarse 2” design significantly lowers the aver-

age price charged to segment {2, 3, 4, 7, 8} (58% of all consumers) while only bringing a modest

price increase for segment {1, 5, 6} (42% of all consumers). Specifically, the former group receives

an average price discount of 21.8% relative to the baseline uniform price—approximately $6 per

game—resulting in substantial welfare gains. In contrast, the latter group sees only a 5.5% price

increase—about $0.89 per game—yielding limited welfare loss. In other words, the optimal “Coarse

2” design causes prices to fall sharply for the majority of types, thereby increasing total quantity

and consumer welfare. This finding is in line with Dub´e and Misra (2023)’s results from a monopoly

market. It is worth noting that our measure of consumer welfare does not incorporate intrinsic pref-

erences for privacy (Lin, 2022) or concerns about price fairness. If these factors were accounted

for, the “Coarse 2” design would likely further approximate—or even surpass—the consumer wel-

fare achieved by the full-information design, while maintaining a clear advantage over the heuristic

approach.

Information symmetry between large versus small sellers. Recent discussions have raised

concerns that larger sellers—owing to their broader product portfolios and longer operating histories—

may possess an informational advantage over smaller sellers. If exploited, this advantage could

allow large sellers to crowd out smaller competitors, ultimately diminishing product variety on the

platform over time.34

In light of this discussion, we examine a concerning asymmetric information structure, where

large sellers (those with more than 25 games) hold and can use full information for targeting, but

the small sellers (25 games or fewer) hold no information and cannot target at all. This represents a

scenario where the platform does not actively design information or imposed common segmentation

for sellers, but instead allows sellers to use their own information about consumers. We compare

this asymmetric targeting case to three key information designs—heuristic “Coarse 2,” optimal

“Coarse 2,” and full information. As we show in Figure 6.5, this asymmetric information scenario

would significantly benefit large sellers at the expense of small sellers. In contrast, the optimal

“Coarse 2” design achieves a more balanced distribution of profit increases across seller sizes, while

also delivering a comparable total profit to the asymmetric case. Therefore, the symmetric, profit-

maximizing “Coarse 2” design also aligns with the platform’s incentive to level the playing field

between large and small sellers.

7 Conclusion

We empirically study a platform’s problem in designing targetable consumer segments for competing

sellers, which we refer to as “platform information design.” Using novel micro data from Steam,

we estimate a flexible demand model that captures heterogeneous consumer demand and develop

a targeted pricing model to simulate equilibrium outcomes under all counterfactual information

designs with discrete consumer types. Because targetable information partitions the market and

changes how sellers compete with each other, accounting for the equilibrium impact is paramount in

information design. To this point, our results demonstrate that the profit-maximizing information

design—which distinguishes heterogeneous consumer types while accounting for its equilibrium

impact—yields substantially higher profits compared to demand-based heuristics that ignore this

equilibrium impact.

Our findings offer important managerial implications for platforms that provide consumer in-

formation to competing sellers, showing that the design of targetable segments is not merely an

exercise that tries to distinguish heterogeneous consumer types. Instead, the platform must also

account for how its information design affects seller competition in equilibrium, especially when it

intends to provide only a limited number of consumer segments to sellers.

A limitation of our study is that we use counterfactual simulations to evaluate alternative in-

formation designs, assuming that sellers set optimal targeted prices given an information structure.

Our approach is necessary because it is challenging for any platform to experimentally vary its

information design and let sellers adjust to a new equilibrium. Nevertheless, evaluating platform

42

Page 44

information design using field or natural experiments would constitute a welcome topic of future

research.

We also have imposed various assumptions to simplify our demand model—including limited

learning about quality or match value, full consideration sets (even though we approximate limited

consideration with flexible demand parameters), and a lack of forward-looking purchase behavior

beyond a fixed horizon. Whereas we present evidence in support of these assumptions in our setting,

migrating our framework to a different context would require one to re-examine these assumptions.

For example, in an evolving market with less experienced consumers, learning or other forms of

demand dynamics may be prevalent, necessitating a different demand model and potentially altering

sellers’ pricing incentives.
