A.2 Number of possible information designs: Derivation

Let X be a finite set consisting of n consumer types in the market. A partition of X can be defined as a

collection of disjoint nonempty type subsets of X, whose union is X. For example, for X = {a, b, c}, there

are 5 possible partitions:

{{a}, {b}, {c}}, {{a, b}, {c}}, {{a, c}, {b}}, {{b, c}, {a}}, {{a, b, c}}.

equation / math rendering (image)
NOTE: contains mathematical notation; text above is the PDF text layer and symbols may be mis-extracted. Image shows the original.

Conceptually, each partition corresponds to a particular information design which constrains how sellers can

target consumer type a, b, and c. Next, we show that the number of possible partitions, and thus information

designs, depends solely on the cardinality of X— n. We denote this number as B(n), which is the n-th Bell

number (Bell, 1934; Rota, 1964).

Proof of the recursive formula for B(n). Consider a set of n+1 elements, and denote the (n+1)-th

element x. Note that for any partition of the set, element x must be in one of the subsets. There are two

possibilities: First, x is in a subset by itself. In this case, the remaining n elements must be partitioned, and

there are B(n) ways to do this. In the second case, x is in a subset with some other elements. To count the

possible partitions in this case, we can partition the n elements into k subsets (k ∈{1, 2, ...n}), and add x

to one of these k subsets. Therefore, we have:

B(n + 1) = B(n) +

B Additional industry details and descriptive patterns

B.1 Competition outside Steam: negligible

One may wonder whether Steam competes against other major platforms. To check the relative size of

Steam to its competitors, we collect search data from Google Trends to compare the number of search

queries for Steam and its major competitors, Origin (developed by Electronic Arts), Epic Store (developed

by Epic Games), and Uplay (developed by Ubisoft). As shown in Figure B.1, the search volume for all three

competitor platforms are negligible compared to that for Steam, confirming Steam’s near-monopoly position

in the PC-gaming market.

Figure B.1: Steam takes a near-monopoly position for PC-based gaming.

Note: In both figures, the gray dotted lines denote the start and end of our sample period. The vertical axis measures the Google search index, normalized by the highest value among the platforms (or games) in comparison.

49

Page 51

We also compare the search for Steam against two major PC games outside of any platform. The first one

is World of Warcraft, released by Blizzard Entertainment in 2004, and the second one is Fortnite, released

by Epic Games in 2017. Both games had low search volumes during our sample period, as the craze for

World of Warcraft had already faded, while the spike of interest in Fortnite had not arrived. Hence, we do

not consider them as major substitutes for games inside Steam.

B.3 Consumer Learning: negligible

One might wonder whether consumer learning plays a significant role in the video game market, especially

given the nature of content goods. If consumers engage in learning— either about product quality or how

well different content features match their preferences— our static demand model could misrepresent the

true distribution of consumer heterogeneity. As discussed in Section 4.1, we argue that learning is minimal

50

Page 52

in the Steam market due to the abundance of information available about game quality and the maturity

of most Steam users. We further validate this claim by examining consumers’ return behavior and their

evolving preferences for content features over time below.

Steam offers a generous return policy, allowing consumers to return a game within two weeks of purchase

(or within two days during game-specific free weekends). As we exclude all returned games from our purchase

panel, we find regular returns account for only 3.8% of initial purchases, suggesting that consumers face

limited uncertainty about game quality. We then analyze whether consumers change their preferences for

game features over time. Specifically, for each consumer, we compare the features of their first five purchases

in the sample period to those of their last five. As shown in Figure B.3, the distributions are largely similar

across consumers, indicating minimal shifts in preferences and suggesting that consumer demand remains

stable during our sample period.

B.4 Pricing patterns on Steam

We examine how typical game prices evolve over time on Steam. To capture the full pricing trajectory, we

focus on the 1,434 games released between January 2015 and December 2018, tracking their price paths

through December 2020 to ensure at least 24 months of observation for each title.

As shown in Figure B.4, a game’s regular (list) price tends to remain stable over time. In contrast,

developers frequently adjust the effective prices through discounts, with the depth of discount gradually

increasing as the game ages. However, unlike the patterns observed in Nair (2007), the overall decline in

effective prices is modest, with little additional change once a game is more than a year old.

Figure B.4: Gradual price decline over time.

Price declines slowly over time. Notably, intertemporal price variation is driven primarily by dis-

counts rather than changes in regular prices. As shown in Figure B.4a, only 25% of games adjust their

regular prices within the first three months after release, while more than half never change their regular

prices within the first two years. Meanwhile, although the average discount increases over time, as shown in

Figure B.4b, the decline is gradual and modest in magnitude.

To further isolate within-game price changes over time, we estimate a regression of game prices on

months since release, controlling for game fixed effects. Table B.2 reports results for three measures: average

monthly price, lowest (effective) monthly price, and maximum monthly discount relative to the release price.

All three measures show a gradual decline post-release. Average and effective prices fall by about $0.07 per

month, with discounts increasing by 0.46% per month. These modest declines suggest that consumers have

limited incentives to delay purchases on Steam, in contrast to the more pronounced intertemporal pricing

effects observed in the console market (Nair, 2007).

C Additional Model Details

C.1 Monte-Carlo Simulation

This subsection validates our demand model through Monte Carlo simulations. We consider a market with

10 video games and two consumer types—–heavy (30% of the market) and light (70% of the market)—–

who differ in purchase intensity, usage intensity, and price sensitivity (Table C.1). Consumers make pur-

chase decisions based on expected future usage and the additional value of expanding their game library.

We simulate consumer purchase and usage behavior for 6000 consumers and 240 days, approximating our

structural sample. We implement estimation for MC = 30.

Table C.1 reports the true parameter values (first column) and compares estimator performance across

four scenarios: estimating on the full simulated sample versus only the latter half, each with and without

modeling the usage stage. When applied to the full data path, the estimator recovers both homogeneous and

heterogeneous parameters without bias. Restricting estimation to the second half—– mirroring our empirical

setting of non-empty initial game libraries—– introduces only minimal bias in the recovered parameters when

the usage stage is modeled.

Finally, we assess whether a model estimated using only purchase-stage data can recover the true dis-

tribution of consumer types. Although the estimator exhibits only minor bias when the full sample is used,

the estimated distribution becomes severely distorted when relying solely on the second half of the sample.

This finding highlights the potential bias of using purchase data alone for estimation, particularly given the

absence of purchase history prior to the start of our sample period.

C.2 Demand-side: Estimation details

This subsection outlines the construction of the sub-sample used for structural estimation, presents the

individual likelihood function based on observed purchases and usage behavior, and describes the selection

of R through model fit comparisons.

Structural sample construction. We retain a final sample of 34, 548 active users who exhibited

both positive spending and usage throughout the sample period and remained on Steam through at least

November 2017. This user sample is used to construct the summary statistics of consumer behavior in

Section 3. Summary statistics on seller pricing patterns, also reported in Section 3, are based on the full

sample of games.

Due to computational constraints, we draw a sub-sample of users and video games for structural estima-

tion. We focus on capturing competition among games that were popular either for purchases or for usage

during the sample period. Thus, we select games that meet one of the following criteria: (1) they are in the

top 70% of expenditure share and have more than 1% of users buying among the 34,548 active users, or (2)

C.3 Supply-side: Solving for the equilibrium prices.

As mentioned in Section 4.2, for each information design, we solve the static pricing equilibrium for each

sampling week separately and then aggregate across weeks. This Section describes how we solve for the

equilibrium prices.

In week tw, a consumer’s choice depends on her library status Li,tw. Because our platform information

design does not permit targeting within the provided segment, solving for the optimal targeted prices requires

an integration over consumers’ libraries. We draw consumer library status from the empirical distribution

when calculating E[sjr,tw] = Ei[sji,tw(Li,tw)|Θr]. Specifically, for the counterfactual targeting scenario with

information sets I, we compute the equilibrium prices P (I) following three steps.

D Additional results

D.1 Demand-side: Estimates and Interpretations

We present the demand estimates in the following order: homogeneous parameters for the usage and purchase

stages, heterogeneous parameters for both stages, and game fixed effects. The left panel of Table D.1 shows

that consumers exhibit significant satiation behavior and face lower time costs on weekends, during summer,

and over holidays—– consistent with increased gameplay during these periods. In the purchase stage, as

shown in the right panel of Table D.1, we find statistically significant positive coefficients for both pre-sale

and sale event periods, suggesting these effects are not driven by inventory stockpiling behavior. Additionally,

we find that the connection between the two stages, σ, is statistically significant, confirming that consumers

take expected future usage into account when making purchase decisions.

Table D.2 presents the game fixed effects with descending order of usage popularity, measured by the

observed total number of usage sessions. Two observations stand out. First, games that are played more

frequently are estimated to have higher usage-stage fixed effects, suggesting that our usage model does capture

revealed consumer preferences. Second, games with higher usage-stage fixed effects are not necessarily

estimated to have high purchase-stage fixed effects. The discrepancy in these two-stage fixed effects reflect

to exhibit higher purchase-stage fixed effects, reflecting the overestimation of game quality at the point of

Figure D.1: Correlation between two-stage FEs: ηj and δj

Additionally, across consumer types, we find that stronger feature preferences correlate weakly with more

negative price sensitivities. This pattern again aligns with algorithmic recommendations, which amplifies

games matching individual tastes in the purchase-stage consideration, rather than with learning behavior

about potential match value with the features. Taken together, the pattern of estimates ˆδj, ˆ λr, and ˆ αr is

closely aligned with the recommendation algorithm instead of consumer learning.

D.2 Supply-side: Generalization

Alternative consumer heterogeneity patterns. Figure D.4 illustrates the two distinct hetero-

geneity patterns uncovered in the decomposition exercise (Section 6.3), while Table D.6 compares the coarse

segmentation formed using optimal information design and the demand-based heuristics under the two coun-

terfactual demand scenarios.

(b) Horizontal heterogeneity: elasticity toward games

Figure D.4: Alternative demand: vertical versus horizontal heterogeneity

Evidently, even under one-dimensional heterogeneity, profit gaps persist across varying levels of granu-

larity. Specifically, when consumer differences are purely vertical (i.e., engagement and price sensitivity)—

that is, a scenario where the sellers are aligned in targeting “strong” and “weak” markets, the elasticity-

based heuristics fail to approximate the optimal design. Similar to Section 6.2, clustering based on vertical

similarity alone isolates the most distinct type, whereas the profit-maximizing design instead pools that type

with others. Moreover, comparison between Table 6.1 and Table D.6 suggests that the optimal “Coarse 2”
